title: Audit your own first fifty reviews
description: Run a genuine self-audit on fifty of your own review decisions — sampling only approved (not corrected) charts — and produce a self-audit report naming your own error pattern with a concrete routine change.

learningObjectives.text: Execute a self-audit sampling and re-review process on real or realistic review data
Identify a genuine personal error pattern and translate it into a concrete routine change

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is lesson five's self-audit, actually run — not designed in the abstract, but performed once, honestly, on a real or realistic set of your own review decisions, with a genuine finding at the end.

contentSections.title: Audit your own first fifty reviews
contentSections.brief: Using fifty of your own past review decisions (from this track's earlier labs and practice work, or a constructed set of fifty realistic chart-and-decision pairs if you don't have real review history yet), run a genuine self-audit: sample from the approved (non-corrected) subset, re-review independently, and identify your own error pattern.
contentSections.deliverable: A self-audit report: the sample you re-reviewed, any discrepancies found between your original and re-reviewed decisions, and — most importantly — a named, specific pattern in what you tend to miss or under-check, plus one concrete change to your personal routine that addresses it.

stages.title: Assemble your fifty and draw your sample
stages.instructions: Gather or construct fifty chart-and-decision pairs representing past review work — real if you have it from this track's earlier labs, constructed and realistic if not. Identify which were approved without correction (the population this audit needs) versus corrected. From the approved subset, draw a genuine sample of at least ten to re-review — random or systematic, not hand-picked for ones you already suspect were fine.
stages.checkpoint: Fifty chart-and-decision pairs exist, the approved subset is clearly identified, and at least ten have been sampled from it without cherry-picking.

stages.title: Re-review the sample independently
stages.instructions: For each sampled chart, re-review from scratch against this phase's verification axes — evidence match, specificity, certainty language, negation, code currency — as if seeing it for the first time, without simply recalling your original reasoning. Note any discrepancy between your original decision and this re-review, and specifically what you missed the first time if there is one.
stages.checkpoint: Every sampled chart has an independent re-review recorded, and any discrepancy is described with the specific detail that was missed, not just flagged as 'different.'

stages.title: Name the pattern and change your routine
stages.instructions: Look across whatever discrepancies you found (including if you found none — that's a real, reportable outcome too, and worth being honest about rather than manufacturing a finding). If you found a pattern — a specific axis you tend to under-check, a specific chart type you rush, a specific kind of hedge language you miss — name it specifically. Then write one concrete change to your personal check routine from lesson four that would address it.
stages.checkpoint: The report either names a specific, evidence-grounded pattern with a concrete routine change, or honestly reports no discrepancies found in this sample with a note on sample-size limits rather than an overstated conclusion either way.

rubric.criterion: The sample is genuinely drawn from approved (not corrected) charts
rubric.meets: At least ten charts sampled specifically from the approved subset, not cherry-picked or drawn from already-corrected charts.

rubric.criterion: Re-review is independent and specific
rubric.meets: Each re-review traces to specific note content, not a restatement of the original decision's reasoning.

rubric.criterion: Any discrepancy is described concretely
rubric.meets: A described discrepancy names the specific detail missed, not a vague 'this one seems off in retrospect.'

rubric.criterion: A named pattern is genuinely evidence-grounded, or absence of one is honestly reported
rubric.meets: The pattern claim traces to more than one specific instance in the sample, or the report explicitly states no pattern was found rather than inventing one.

rubric.criterion: The routine change is concrete and addresses the specific pattern
rubric.meets: The proposed change names a specific addition or adjustment to the lesson-four routine, not a general resolution to 'be more careful.'

rubric.criterion: The report is honest about limitations
rubric.meets: Acknowledges sample size and what this audit can and can't conclude, rather than overstating certainty from a small sample.

contentSections.body: A self-audit that finds nothing is a real, useful result, not a wasted exercise — and a self-audit that finds a genuine pattern, named specifically and turned into a routine change, is the module's entire point in one document.

title: Checkpoint — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode

questions.from: This module — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
questions.prompt: What is automation bias, in this context?

options.label: Trust in a system's general track record eroding vigilance specifically where it matters most — on the review queue's self-selected hard cases
A technical flaw in how confidence scores are calculated
A deliberate policy of trusting AI systems less over time

questions.explanation: It's a well-documented, broadly human response — a real track record misapplied to a population (the queue) it was never actually measured on.

questions.from: This module — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
questions.prompt: What's the key behavioral difference between a genuine verification and a rubber-stamp approval?

options.label: Genuine verification traces the decision back to specific note content; a rubber stamp substitutes a proxy like a confidence score or general familiarity
Genuine verification always takes over five minutes
There's no real difference if both end in 'approve'

questions.explanation: The two can look identical from the outside — the difference is entirely in whether the decision could be justified by citing specific documentation.

questions.from: This module — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
questions.prompt: Why does a volume target borrowed from manual coding benchmarks misapply to a review queue?

options.label: It's based on a mixed, mostly-routine workload, while the queue is a self-selected, structurally harder subset
It doesn't misapply — the same number works for both
Manual coders were always slower than reviewers

questions.explanation: The same throughput number implies much less time per genuinely hard chart when applied to a queue that's already had the routine cases filtered out.

questions.from: This module — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
questions.prompt: What's the single design principle that matters most for a personal check routine surviving a bad day?

options.label: Low cognitive load — short and memorable enough to run without active recall of complex rules
Maximum comprehensiveness, covering every possible edge case
Being written down in a long reference document

questions.explanation: A routine that's hard to even remember on a foggy day won't get run — everything else about it becomes irrelevant if it doesn't survive being run at all.

questions.from: This module — The Reviewer's Own Failure Mode
questions.prompt: Why can't correction-rate tracking alone detect automation bias?

options.label: It only records errors the reviewer already caught, not errors that were missed and silently approved
Correction tracking is always inaccurate
It can detect automation bias perfectly well on its own

questions.explanation: A missed error, by definition, was never flagged as a correction — only an independent re-review of approved charts (a self-audit) can surface that population.

questions.from: Previous module — How the AI Assigns a Code
questions.prompt: What does a confidence score actually measure?

options.label: A calibrated real-world probability the code is correct
How closely the note's language matches patterns the model associates with that code from training
The provider's certainty in their own diagnosis

questions.explanation: It's a similarity-to-training-patterns signal, correlated with but not identical to a calibrated probability of correctness.

questions.from: Previous module — How the AI Assigns a Code
questions.prompt: Why does a pipeline systematically favor less specific codes even when more specific ones are documented?

options.label: Real-world documentation under-specifies more often than it over-specifies, and the model absorbed the same asymmetry
It's a random, unpatterned error
Specific codes are technically harder to generate

questions.explanation: The bias is data-driven, tracing to an asymmetry already present in the historical documentation the pipeline trained on.

questions.from: Previous module — How the AI Assigns a Code
questions.prompt: Why are negation-scope errors harder for a reviewer to catch than an unmentioned-concept error?

options.label: The negated concept genuinely appears in the note, just denied, so a quick scan for the concept finds it and moves on
They're actually easier to catch
Negated findings are always formatted in bold

questions.explanation: Confirming a concept is mentioned isn't the same as confirming it's asserted as present — that gap is exactly where negation errors hide.

questions.from: Three modules back — What This Role Actually Is
questions.prompt: Why is the review queue not a random sample of all encounters?

options.label: It's the pipeline's own low-confidence and rule-flagged output, concentrated together — not a random draw
It's a random 10% sample for quality assurance
It's every chart above a certain dollar value

questions.explanation: Everything the pipeline was confident about auto-submits without a human; what's left over-represents ambiguity and contradiction by construction.

questions.from: Three modules back — What This Role Actually Is
questions.prompt: What does approving an AI-proposed code actually attest to?

options.label: That, in your professional judgment, the code matches what this specific chart's documentation supports
That the AI's confidence score was accurate
That no further review will ever be needed on this chart

questions.explanation: Your approval is a professional judgment about this specific chart — not a comment on the AI's process, which is why 'the AI proposed it' isn't a valid defense later.

contentSections.body: This is the last checkpoint of the phase — a phase review, pulling across all five modules with a transfer question, comes next. Anything that didn't come back here is fair game there.
